title: H²CL: Heterogeneity-Aware Hypergraph Learning
one_liner: When learning from hypergraphs, detect which connections mix incompatible node types and downweight them to avoid training on mixed signals.
lead: Hypergraphs connect multiple nodes through a single hyperedge (unlike regular graphs, which connect exactly two). Most learning methods assume all nodes in one hyperedge are similar, but real hypergraphs mix different types together—a email hyperedge might group a person, a company domain, and a spam tag. This paper detects that mixing and learns to ignore those unreliable connections.

paras: A hyperedge is just a group of nodes (like an email thread with a person, a topic, and a time). Older methods pretend all nodes in that group are similar—they treat the person, topic, and time as if they belong to the same category.

In real data, that is wrong. A single hyperedge often groups incompatible things: a social network hyperedge might connect a celebrity (famous) with a random user (unknown) and a bot (automated). The learning algorithm sees all three as one group, learns that they are similar, and gets confused when it later sees those nodes in different combinations.

callout.html: Methods assume all nodes in a hyperedge are alike, but real hyperedges mix different types, poisoning the learning signal.

hidden.h2: Heterogeneity: how mixed is this group?
hidden.name: node-hyperedge heterogeneity
paras: Heterogeneity measures how different a node is from the typical node in its hyperedge. If a hyperedge connects a celebrity with a random user, the two have high heterogeneity (very different). If it connects two similar users, heterogeneity is low.

The paper estimates this by looking at node features (the numbers describing each node). For each node, it computes the distance from that node to the center of the hyperedge. A big distance means that node does not fit the group's pattern—heterogeneity is high.

heat.caption: Darker means more different from the hyperedge group average (higher heterogeneity).

reads.html: Some nodes fit the hyperedge pattern; others do not. This paper measures that mismatch.
The paper estimates node-hyperedge heterogeneity from features, then uses it to selectively mask incidences (connections) and reweight aggregation.

paras: When two very different nodes are forced into the same learning group, the algorithm tries to make them similar. That creates a false pattern. If a celebrity and a bot are both labeled as part of one hyperedge, the learning algorithm believes celebrities and bots should be treated alike—wrong.

By measuring heterogeneity and downweighting mixed connections, the algorithm stops trying to align incompatible nodes. The celebrity's list of features (numbers describing it) stays far from the bot's list, so the algorithm correctly learns that they are separate types. Message-passing (information shared between nodes) also becomes more reliable because a node only listens to neighbors that fit its group's pattern, filtering out noise—when it hears only from compatible nodes, it learns their actual shared properties instead of averaging across incompatible types.

stages.s: Measure distance from each node to hyperedge center
Mark nodes far from center as high-heterogeneity
Clean learning signal, no false alignments

math.words: For each connection in the hyperedge, apply a reweight factor based on how different the connected node is from the hyperedge average, so that mixed-type connections contribute less to learning.
math.equation: h_weighted = sum_e w(e) * agg(v in e) where w(e) = 1 - heterogeneity(v,e)
symbols: the learned representation after heterogeneity reweighting
the weight of hyperedge e based on how mixed it is
aggregate (combine) all node features in hyperedge e
how different node v is from the average of hyperedge e (range 0-1)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Hyperedge E contains three nodes: Person (features at the center), Bot (far from center), Celebrity (far from center).
Person-to-E heterogeneity: 0.1 (fits the group). Bot-to-E: 0.8 (outlier). Celebrity-to-E: 0.7 (outlier).
When aggregating E, Person's update is scaled by 0.9 (trusted), Bot by 0.2 (suppressed), Celebrity by 0.3 (suppressed).
Result: the model learns from Person's signal, ignores the mixed types.

math.note: The weight becomes small (close to 0) when heterogeneity is high, so mixed-type nodes contribute less to learning.

items.html: If the features do not capture what makes nodes compatible or incompatible, heterogeneity will mismeasure the mixing problem. For example, if node features are all near zero (weak signal), distance becomes noise, and the paper's mask throws away good edges by mistake.
A hyperedge with only two nodes has no reliable center. If the paper masks one node as high-heterogeneity, it removes half the hyperedge, leaving no signal at all.

The paper must decide how high heterogeneity must be to mask a connection. A threshold that works for one dataset (a social network) may fail for another (a document network), masking too much or too little.
When features are informative and hyperedges have enough nodes to find a reliable center, heterogeneity correctly identifies and suppresses mixed-type connections, leaving the learning signal clean.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic hypergraph where each hyperedge is labeled as either compatible (all nodes from the same category) or mixed (nodes from different categories intentionally grouped). Train a model with the old method (no heterogeneity) and with H²CL. Then corrupt a test hypergraph by adding random mixed edges. The old method should drop in accuracy; H²CL should stay stable. Plot accuracy versus corruption level on both.
demo.closing: The demo must show that when edges are intentionally noisy, the old method fails but H²CL keeps learning.
